Definition: Whether individuals can view their data held in the ID database and see how it has been accessed
Comments: Niger's Law No. 2022-59 (Data Protection Act, Article 69) grants data subjects the right to access: confirmation of whether personal data is processed, a copy of their personal data, information on data origins, purposes of processing, and recipients. This right of individual access to personal data held in identity systems is enshrined in law.
revision_notes: Fetched the cited DLA Piper and Caseguard pages, which confirm Niger's data protection legal framework but do not themselves detail the right-of-access provision. A targeted search located and fetched the HAPDP's own website, which sets out the right of access under Article 27 (rather than Article 69) of the consolidated data protection law. The substantive right - individuals may obtain confirmation of whether their data are processed, a copy of the data, and information on origin, purpose and recipients - is confirmed directly by the data protection authority itself. Score of 2 (Yes) confirmed on this corrected legal basis.
revised_comments: Niger's consolidated data protection law (Law No. 2022-59 of 16 December 2022) grants data subjects a right of access under Article 27, entitling individuals to obtain confirmation of whether their personal data are processed, a copy of the data held, and information on its origin, purpose and recipients. The Haute Autorite de Protection des Donnees a caractere Personnel (HAPDP) publishes this right on its official website, confirming that individuals can view data held about them, including within identity systems.

Definition: Whether the ID authority and system are subject to general oversight of the courts and judicial review
Value Name: Yes, but not specific to ID
Comments: Decisions of the HAPDP (data protection authority) are subject to appeal before the Conseil d'État (Council of State) per the 2022 Personal Data Protection Act. This provides judicial oversight over data protection decisions affecting digital ID. No dedicated ID-specific judicial oversight mechanism has been identified in available sources.
revision_notes: Fetched the cited Le Sahel article and DLA Piper page, plus a Wikipedia (French) profile of the HAPDP located via a targeted search and fetched in full. All confirm that HAPDP decisions are administrative acts that can be appealed before the Conseil d'Etat, Niger's supreme administrative court. This is general judicial oversight of the data protection authority, not an ID-specific mechanism, matching the original assessment. No evidence was found of any ID-specific judicial review channel. Score of 2 confirmed.
revised_comments: Decisions of Niger's Haute Autorite de Protection des Donnees a caractere Personnel (HAPDP) are administrative acts subject to appeal before the Conseil d'Etat, Niger's highest administrative court. This provides general judicial oversight of the data protection authority's rulings, including those affecting personal data held in identity systems, but this oversight derives from the general administrative law framework rather than from any ID-specific judicial mechanism.

Definition: Whether procedural rules for collection, storage, and sharing of ID-related personal data are publicly available and established
Comments: Law No. 2022-59 of 16 December 2022 (Data Protection Act) establishes data sharing rules requiring prior consent, purpose limitation, and notification of data subjects about third-party data sharing. Cross-border transfers require equivalent protection. Processing requires prior notification to HAPDP. Rules are codified in law but specific operational data sharing frameworks for the ID system are not fully published.
revision_notes: Fetched the cited DLA Piper and Caseguard pages, plus the HAPDP's own website (Articles 26-32) located via search and fetched directly, which sets out detailed procedural rules on prior information to data subjects, consent, purpose limitation and cross-border transfer restrictions. These general rules are publicly hosted by the regulator itself. However, no dedicated, ID-system-specific data-sharing agreement or operational framework (e.g. for the WURI identification system) was found published separately, so the rules remain general rather than ID-specific. Score of 2 (Partially available) confirmed; a promotion to 3 (Fully available, the top of this scale) was considered but not made given the absence of ID-specific published documentation.
revised_comments: Niger's data protection law (Law No. 2022-59 of 16 December 2022) sets out detailed rules, published by the regulator itself, on the collection, storage and sharing of personal data, including prior information obligations to data subjects (Article 26), the right of access (Article 27), consent and purpose-limitation requirements, and provisions governing transfers to third countries. These general rules apply to personal data held within the identity system, though no dedicated, ID-specific data-sharing framework has been identified separately.

Definition: Whether national data protection legislation exists and covers personal data linked to the ID system
Comments: Niger has a comprehensive data protection law: Law No. 2017-28 of 3 May 2017 on Protection of Personal Data, subsequently amended by Law No. 2019-71 of 24 December 2019, Law No. 2022-59 of 16 December 2022 (new consolidated act), and Law No. 2023-31 of 4 July 2023. The law governs collection, processing, storage and transfer of personal data including biometric data.
revision_notes: Fetched all three cited sources. DLA Piper (last modified January 2025) confirms the legislative lineage cited. Le Sahel adds that the framework has been further amended by ordonnances 2024-16 (26 April 2024) and 2024-29 (24 June 2024) to align with technological developments, and clarifies that Law No. 2022-59 repealed rather than merely amended the 2017/2019 framework, though the substantive conclusion is unaffected. Score of 2 (Yes) confirmed; year updated to reflect the most recent confirmed legislative amendment found.
revised_comments: Niger's data protection legislation, originally Law No. 2017-28 of 3 May 2017, was repealed and replaced by the consolidated Law No. 2022-59 of 16 December 2022, itself amended by Law No. 2023-31 of 4 July 2023 and further amending ordonnances (2024-16 of 26 April 2024 and 2024-29 of 24 June 2024). The law establishes comprehensive rules governing the collection, processing and transfer of personal data, including biometric data, and thus covers personal data linked to the digital ID system.

Definition: Whether a Data Protection Authority or similar body regulates ID data collection and sharing by the ID system
Comments: The Haute Autorité de Protection des Données à caractère Personnel (HAPDP) was established by Law No. 2017-28 of 3 May 2017 and became operational in 2020. It is an independent administrative authority attached to the Presidency of the Republic, responsible for ensuring compliance with data protection law. The Ministry of Interior consulted the HAPDP regarding the WURI unique identification process (2024). The HAPDP has a strategic plan 2021-2025.
revision_notes: Fetched all three cited sources plus a Wikipedia (French) profile of the HAPDP located via search and fetched in full. All confirm the HAPDP was created by Law No. 2017-28 of 2017, became operational in 2020, and remains an active independent administrative authority attached to the Presidency, with investigative, authorisation and sanctioning powers under the current law, including consultation on the WURI identification process. Score of 2 (Yes) confirmed; year updated to the most recent confirmed evidence of active oversight.
revised_comments: The Haute Autorite de Protection des Donnees a caractere Personnel (HAPDP), established under Law No. 2017-28 of 2017 and operational since 2020, is Niger's independent data protection authority. It regulates data collection and sharing across public and private sectors, issues authorisations and opinions - including consultation on the WURI unique identification process - and its decisions carry enforceable administrative sanctions under the current data protection law.
